clue.text: Neat Conservative PM no longer? Back off!

indicators.note: the back of the name, its final letter, comes off

parts.note: Clement Attlee was a British prime minister, so he is a PM no longer

explanation.surface: A tidy former Tory prime minister is told to retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back off' drops the last E of ATTLEE. 'Neat' is the old word for oxen and cows, not tidy; Attlee was Labour, so 'Conservative' is just C.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat is an archaic or dialect word for bovine livestock, cows and oxen kept on a farm.

clue.text: Related to heat that's somewhat tropical — or Icelandic?

indicators.note: somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A question whether something is a bit tropical or rather Icelandic in its temperature.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition took in 'that's', which only links the definition to 'somewhat'; the definition is 'Related to heat'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things concerning heat or calories, as in the old caloric theory of warmth as a fluid.

clue.text: Fancy a malt? Test old whiskey with new label

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are arranged in a new way

parts.note: the MOT is the annual UK roadworthiness test for vehicles
Whiskey is the NATO alphabet code word for the letter W

explanation.surface: A drinker is invited to try an aged whiskey sold under a fresh brand label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an invitation ('Fancy a drink?') but is the anagram signal for 'a malt'. The MOT is the British annual car safety test.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the Detroit record company of the Supremes and Stevie Wonder, so a record label.

clue.text: Become visibly cheerful, seeing broadcast plug hit

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone brightens on seeing a hit record being plugged on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A face that brightens shows happiness openly, the idiom for becoming visibly happy.

clue.text: Witnessed retreat, with soldiers returning

indicators.note: returning means the whole run of letters comes back, read backwards

parts.note: a den is a private retreat or hideaway
GIs are American soldiers

explanation.surface: Someone saw a military withdrawal as the troops came home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Witnessed' here means put one's name to a document as a witness, not merely saw.
explanation.definitionFit: A witness to a will or contract adds a signature, so to have witnessed a document is to have put your name on it.

clue.text: Cut use of heroin, finally going for Hitsville's No 1

indicators.note: the use of something here means it is put to work and reworked, so the letters are rearranged
one letter going for another means it takes its place
the number one letter of a word is its first
finally points to the very end letter of the word

explanation.surface: A call to cut out heroin use, with a record company's top single as the substitute.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'heroin' the H, first letter of Hitsville (Hitsville U.S.A. was the record company's Detroit headquarters), is swapped for G, the last letter of 'going', and the result is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut someone is to snub them, deliberately pretending not to see or know them.

clue.text: Fruitful product of internecine war is losing weight for a short time

wordplay.reading: T for W in WAR inter NECINE

parts.words: internecine war is losing weight for a short time
parts.note: internecine is read as inter, between, plus necine; war, swapping W for weight for T for a short time, becomes tar and is put between

explanation.surface: Something grows out of a mutually destructive war that is briefly shedding pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: One clue word does two jobs: 'internecine' reads as INTER (put between) followed by the letters it acts on, and 'is losing ... for' swaps W, weight, for T, a short time.
explanation.definitionFit: A smooth-skinned peach is the crop of a fruit tree, so it is a product of fruiting.

clue.text: River with poster that's never even got onto a sort of fishing

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland, and another in Wales and England

indicators.note: never taking the even letters leaves the odd ones, first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: A river angler with a billboard that never quite levels out takes up fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishing far out in the open ocean, for marlin or tuna, is a recognised style of the sport.

clue.text: Oddly brown — as sap, in small pot plant?

indicators.note: oddly means take the odd-numbered letters, first, third, fifth and so on

explanation.surface: A little potted plant has turned brown, as if its sap were in trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art keeps a tree dwarfed in a shallow container, so it is a miniature potted tree.

clue.text: Harshly criticize second hit

parts.note: to lam is to thrash or beat someone

explanation.surface: A critic savages a second-rate hit song.
explanation.definitionFit: Critics who pan a play or film savagely are said to do this in informal usage.

clue.text: Airport staff dreadfully rude? Wrong, when keeping cool head

indicators.note: keeping means holding something inside
dreadfully says the letters are mangled into a new order
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Rude airport workers are told off, though they keep their cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' looks like a second anagram signal but is fodder; 'dreadfully' scrambles both words, and 'when keeping' holds the C inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The workers who refuel, load and service planes on the apron are the airfield's support team on land.

clue.text: Mostly loyal worker becomes absentee

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word, so it loses its last letter

parts.note: true means loyal, as in a true friend
the worker ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: A faithful employee turns into someone who no longer shows up.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil who skips school without permission is one who is missing from class.

clue.text: Some flipping moss, a grass, or seaweed

indicators.note: flipping says the hidden letters are read backwards
Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An exasperated speaker lumps together moss, grass or seaweed.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition took in 'or', which only links; the definition is 'seaweed'. 'flipping' looks like a mild curse but is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A brown floating alga of the Atlantic gives its name to the Sargasso Sea, so the name is a kind of seaweed.

clue.text: Playing a simple chord, initially without a complaint

indicators.note: without, in its old sense of outside, means the shuffled letters go round this one
playing about with the letters rearranges them
initially points to the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone strumming an easy chord is free of any grumbles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without', in its old sense of outside, puts the shuffled letters round the first A; the second A ends the answer. 'complaint' is a medical one, not a grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a serious pregnancy condition with convulsions; complaint is used in its sense of an illness or ailment.

clue.text: Tabloids regularly feature this corrupt Tory's goal

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or perverted, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Popular newspapers keep running stories on a crooked Conservative's ambition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' is not an every-other-letter signal here: it is part of the definition, saying how often tabloids run horoscopes.
explanation.definitionFit: Popular newspapers carry a daily horoscope page, star-sign forecasts being a regular feature.

clue.text: Fizzy drink will briefly give you zip

parts.note: soda is a carbonated drink
the contraction of will is 'll, as in you'll

explanation.surface: A fizzy drink is promised to give you energy and pep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'zip' looks like pep or energy, but here it is slang for nothing at all, as in 'zip, zilch'. The answer is British slang for nothing whatever.
explanation.definitionFit: Zip is American slang for nothing, a synonym of the British vulgar phrase meaning not a thing.

clue.text: See 15
When finally very keen to get back in bed

indicators.note: getting back means the word is turned round, read backwards

parts.note: avid means very keen or eager

indicators.note: finally points to the very end letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone who is eager to return to bed at the end of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: A low backless couch or sofa that serves as a bed is a kind of bed.

clue.text: Checks case for source of smelly underwear

indicators.note: a case encloses its contents, so this word goes round the next piece

parts.note: to vet is to check or examine

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it starts, its first letter

explanation.surface: An inspector looks into what makes some underclothes smell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case for' puts VETS round S, the source of 'smelly'. In British use these are undershirts, not waistcoats.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain the word means sleeveless undershirts, garments worn next to the skin.

clue.text: Cake counter's surprisingly lacking 15 16

indicators.note: surprisingly says the letters turn up in an unexpected order
lacking means one letter is missing from the pool before it is rearranged

parts.note: the linked answer means nothing, and O is the letter that looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A cake shop counter is, to everyone's surprise, completely empty.
explanation.walkthrough: Take O, nothing, from the letters of COUNTERS and rearrange the rest. 'Cake' is a verb here, to coat with a hard layer.
explanation.definitionFit: To cake something is to coat it with a hardened layer, as mud cakes boots; both words mean form a crust.

clue.text: Rescued organ dumped in river, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: says the answer is said like the phrase built, not spelt like it

parts.note: a liver (an organ) thrown into the Dee (a river) is fancifully Dee-livered

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a body part was rescued after being dropped in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dee is a river in Britain; dropping a liver into it gives a punning 'Dee-livered', which is said like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver someone from danger is to save or set them free, as in 'deliver us from evil'.

clue.text: Casually spinning lie, say

indicators.note: spinning turns the letters round into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone tells a fib in an offhand way, by way of example.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something casually means doing it without strain or effort, in a relaxed way.

clue.text: Contrary way poets work

definitions.meaning: contrary means opposite, reversed in direction
poets write in lines of metre, read as a two-word phrase saying in metre

explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer says how poets write: in metre.
explanation.definitionFit: An opposite proposition or relation is its contrary, and poets compose in metrical lines.

clue.text: Called for more to come from the heart, ultimately?

indicators.note: the heart comes from within, so this piece sits in the middle of the other

parts.note: the end is what comes ultimately, at the last
the core is the heart of something

explanation.surface: An audience demand for more that comes, in the end, straight from the heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to come from' puts CORE, the heart, in the middle of END.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience that shouts for an extra song at the close of a show is demanding another performance.

clue.text: See 2
One refrain contains 15 16 relating to Greek god's blood

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: contains means the word holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: the chorus is the refrain of a song
the linked answer means nothing, and O is the letter that looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A single song refrain turns out to say nothing about mythology.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth ichor is the ethereal fluid that runs in the veins of the gods.
explanation.definitionFit: Ichor is the golden fluid flowing in immortals' veins, and the adjective describes things concerning it.

clue.text: City even mice deserted originally?

indicators.note: the original letters, the first of each word, desert them and are dropped

explanation.surface: A question whether a city was abandoned even by its mice in the beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deserted originally' removes the opening letters, E and M, leaving VEN and ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian lagoon port of canals and gondolas is a famous city.

clue.text: Country with China as neighbour to north-east

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits just above the other, its neighbour

parts.note: china is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, from china plate, so a pal

explanation.surface: A Himalayan land has the Chinese state as its neighbour across the north-east border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is not the country but rhyming slang: china plate rhymes with mate. Nepal really does border China to the north.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan kingdom, now a republic, between India and Tibet is a sovereign nation.

clue.text: Our ordeal involved getting hold of lost deposit in foreign bank

indicators.note: getting hold of means grasping, so these letters take the next piece inside
involved means tangled or convoluted, so the letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for lost, as in sports results tables

explanation.surface: A traveller's ordeal involves losing a deposit at an overseas bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges OUR ORDEAL; 'getting hold of' then takes in L for lost.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a US currency deposit held in a bank outside America, so money lodged abroad.

clue.text: Standard recipe for salmon

parts.note: par is a standard or norm, as in up to par
R is the abbreviation for recipe, from the Latin on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A standard method for cooking salmon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recipe' gives R, the old prescription abbreviation for Latin recipe, 'take'.
explanation.definitionFit: A young salmon in its first stage in fresh water, with dark bars on its sides, has this name.

clue.text: Playing together, except for number about one that's Scottish

indicators.note: about means going round the next piece
except for means leave out what follows

parts.note: a number here is something that numbs, and ether is an anaesthetic
yin is the Scots word for one

explanation.surface: Children playing nicely together, except for one number about a Scot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number' is what numbs, ETHER, not a figure: 'together' minus ETHER is TOG, which goes 'about' YIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing with an idea means dallying or trifling with it, without serious intent.

clue.text: Tied up, in case ale drunk

indicators.note: in says the answer lies inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A drunk is tied up while a case of beer is consumed.
explanation.definitionFit: A deal tied up is one concluded and settled, closed like an envelope.
